title: Nasogastric (NG) Tube Insertion
summary: Inserting a nasogastric tube for feeding, medication administration, or gastric decompression.
equipment: Cup of water with straw (if patient can swallow)
steps: Verify order and assess for contraindications (facial trauma, esophageal varices, recent surgery).
Elevate HOB to 45–90°. Assess nares — choose the more patent side.
Measure tube length: earlobe → tip of nose → xiphoid process. Mark or note the measurement.
Lubricate the first 3–4 inches of the tube with water-soluble lubricant.
Don gloves. Insert tube through nare and advance posteriorly — aim toward ear, not top of head.
Advance tube while asking patient to swallow (or tilt chin to chest). If gagging is excessive, pause and allow to pass.
Monitor for respiratory distress, cyanosis, or inability to speak — if these occur, remove immediately.
Advance to the marked measurement. Secure tube temporarily.
Verify placement by: (1) aspirating gastric contents and checking pH ≤ 5.5 or using CO2 detector, (2) X-ray confirmation before first feeding.
Do NOT rely solely on air insufflation (whoosh test) — not reliable.
Secure tube to nose with tape or commercial holder. Mark tube at nare exit point.
Document insertion, tube length at nare, confirmation method, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: X-ray is the gold standard for confirmation before initiating feeds.
Recheck tube placement before each feeding and medication administration.
Assess nare for pressure injury — rotate side if long-term use.
Never insert in patients with basilar skull fracture — use OG tube instead.
Monitor for tube migration, especially after coughing or vomiting episodes.

title: Gastrostomy / PEG Tube Care & Feeding
summary: Caring for a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube and administering enteral feedings.
equipment: Enteral feeding pump and tubing (for continuous feeds)
steps: Verify tube feeding order: formula type, rate, schedule, and flushing protocol.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Assess tube exit site: redness, granulation tissue, leakage, skin breakdown.
Gently clean around the site with warm water and mild soap. Dry thoroughly.
Rotate the tube 360° once daily (unless a balloon-type G-tube — do not rotate).
Check external tube length/markings to confirm no migration since last assessment.
Before feeding: check residual volume by aspirating stomach contents. If residual is >200–500 mL (per policy), hold feed and notify provider.
Aspirate and check pH if tube placement is in question (gastric pH ≤5.5).
Flush tube with 30 mL water before feeding.
Administer formula via gravity or pump at prescribed rate. Keep HOB elevated ≥30°.
Flush with 30 mL water after feeding and before/after each medication administration.
Crush and dissolve medications separately. Never mix medications with formula.
Document site assessment, residual volume, volume administered, and patient tolerance.
nursing_considerations: Blue/green food coloring in enteral feedings is no longer recommended — it has been associated with patient deaths.
Keep HOB elevated ≥30° during and for 30–60 minutes after feedings — prevents aspiration.
Never administer feedings into a jejunostomy tube at gastric rates — jejunum cannot tolerate high bolus volumes.
Medications must be liquid form or fully dissolved before administration — crushed tablet clumps can clog tube.
A clogged tube can often be cleared with warm water and a 60mL syringe using gentle back-and-forth pressure — never use a wire stylet.

title: Ostomy Care (Colostomy / Ileostomy)
summary: Emptying and changing a fecal ostomy pouching system and assessing the stoma.
equipment: One-piece or two-piece ostomy pouching system
steps: Gather all supplies. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Empty the ostomy pouch: open the clamp/tail closure at the bottom, drain into toilet. Wipe the end clean and re-clamp.
If changing the pouch: gently remove entire system using one hand to press skin down while lifting pouch up — never rip.
Note stoma color, shape, height, and any signs of complication.
Assess peristomal skin: redness, erosion, hyperplasia, fistula, retraction.
Cleanse stoma and surrounding skin with warm water. A small amount of mild soap is acceptable. Rinse and pat dry completely.
Measure stoma with the guide. Cut the barrier opening 2–3 mm larger than the stoma to allow for peristalsis.
Apply skin barrier paste around the stoma if needed (fills uneven surfaces to prevent leakage).
Apply skin prep wipe and allow to dry.
Warm the skin barrier between your hands for 30 seconds to improve adhesion.
Center the pouch over the stoma and press firmly for 30–60 seconds from inner to outer edges.
Close the tail/clamp at the bottom. Smooth out the pouch.
Document stoma assessment, output characteristics (color, consistency, amount), and skin condition.
nursing_considerations: Healthy stoma should be beefy red/pink and moist — notify provider immediately for pale, blue, or black stoma.
Ileostomy output is liquid-green, high volume, and enzymatic — highly corrosive to skin if it leaks.
Colostomy output varies by location: ascending = liquid; transverse = semi-formed; descending/sigmoid = formed.
Change pouching system every 3–5 days or immediately if leaking — 'just adding tape' around a leak delays skin breakdown.
Assess for parastomal hernia: bulge around stoma when patient bears down; report to provider, modify pouch system.

title: Enema Administration
summary: Instilling solution into the rectum and colon to relieve constipation, cleanse the bowel, or administer medications.
equipment: Enema kit (bag/container, tubing with rectal tip) or pre-packaged enema (Fleet)
Enema solution per order (NS, tap water, soapsuds, mineral oil, or medicated)
steps: Verify provider order: type of enema, volume, and retention time if applicable.
Explain procedure to patient. Provide privacy.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Prepare enema solution at room temperature (105–110°F for adults). Clamp tubing.
Position patient in left Sims' position (left lateral with right knee drawn toward chest) — aligns with rectum anatomy.
Place waterproof pad under the patient's buttocks.
Lubricate the rectal tip generously.
Gently separate buttocks and insert rectal tip 3–4 inches (adult) into the rectum, aimed toward the umbilicus.
Open clamp. Raise bag 12–18 inches above rectum and allow solution to flow slowly.
If patient reports cramping, lower the bag or clamp tubing briefly until cramping subsides, then continue.
Administer prescribed volume. Clamp tubing and remove rectal tip smoothly.
Instruct patient to retain enema as long as possible (at least 5–15 minutes or per order).
Assist patient to bedpan or bathroom. Do NOT leave a patient with severe cramping or urgency unattended.
Document type, volume instilled, patient tolerance, and results (stool character and amount).
nursing_considerations: Contraindications: recent rectal/bowel surgery, inflamed bowel disease (Crohn's/UC flare), bowel obstruction, rectal bleeding, hemorrhoids (use caution).
Never give enemas to patients with a recent bowel anastomosis without explicit surgical order.
Cleansing enemas may need to be repeated until return is clear — follow order carefully.
Hypertonic phosphate enemas (Fleet) can cause dangerous electrolyte shifts — avoid in renal failure or elderly.
Do not force the rectal tip if resistance is felt — could indicate impaction or tumor.
